cues.text: Hi Liz. How do you feel about starting university here?
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: A little bit nervous, but I’m confident I can handle it. This orientation program seems like it will help us a lot.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Sure. I’m looking at the timetable here myself. It seems that there are choices available.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: I can see. So, what are you going to do Monday afternoon? In the morning we all have the opening lecture, but it looks like we have a choice later that day, as you said.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Well, the ‘Careers Lecture’ might be helpful, but I am interested in the ‘Uni Tour’. It’s probably too early to be thinking of careers now, anyway, and I want to know what’s what at this new university, so I’m doing the tour.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Alright. I’ll come along with you. Might learn something interesting. After all, we haven’t seen much of this place yet, and we will be spending four years here.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Tuesday is another full day, too. In the afternoon there’s a lecture about study skills, but that morning offers another choice.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: ‘Library Tour’ or ‘Student Union Induction’. What do you think?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: I think the student union is very important, but we can go there any time, right, so we should take advantage of the library tour while it’s being offered. Maybe the week after, you and I can go to the student union.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Library it is, then. Now, Wednesday has a free session in the morning, but after lunch there’s a choice between visiting the computer lab, or attending a lecture on our legal rights.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Well, law and rights are important, but computers are the basis of everything these days, so I’m going to the computer lab.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Don’t you think knowing our legal rights is equally, if not more, important? We live in a very litigious and complex society now.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Sure, but it’s something we can pick up later, so let’s leave that one out.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Okay.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Let me see the timetable. Thursday is a free day, and the week winds up with some celebrations on Friday afternoon. It looks like a fun choice, too. There’s either a BBQ on the main lawn, or the dance.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: I never pass up the chance to eat something. What about you?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: If I can get a free meal, I’ll take it any day, and I’m not good at dancing anyway.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Well, that’s that decided. Right?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Right!
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Guess what Liz? There’s another interesting thing in this orientation booklet, and it looks important -about a ‘style guide’.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: What’s that?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Take a look yourself. It seems to be a set of rules regarding how to present written work - essays, and that sort of thing - to the lecturers. They want a uniform style of presentation.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: I can see. So, everything we hand in must have a header and a footer.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: A what?
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: A header and a footer. The footer is at the bottom of the page, and the header is at the very top. That’s why they call it a ‘header’, you know, that little bit of writing giving details about the work. And they also want the word count. Why do they need that?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: I guess because the lecturers will specify the number of words they want for their assignment, and they want to be sure students follow this.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: And even the heading on the page has to be a specific dimension. 16 points, and bold print, and underlined.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: And subheadings are 14 points, and the font has to be Arial for everything.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Yes, the main text is Arial, too, as you said, and the size is 12 points, with the header and footer being slightly smaller, at 10 points each. Well, it seems logical. The size of everything is in proportion to its importance, but why do they need the spacing of the main text to be one and a half?The header and footer are different. They’re only single-spaced.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Probably to allow the teacher to insert comments, or corrections, or just to make it all more readable, I suppose.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: And we need wide margins on the left, right, top, and bottom, probably for the same reason. Lots of space to allow the addition of comments. That’s a bit scary, actually. It seems to assume we will be making mistakes.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: And look what they want in the header and footer. The header has the name of the work.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Not the name of the teacher?
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: No, the work, but surely the teacher’s name must go somewhere. Ah, here it is. It goes in the footer.
cues.speaker: Sam

cues.text: Okay, I’d say this is all logical. If a page is lost, say, falls to the floor, then with all this information, it can always be traced back to the teacher involved.
cues.speaker: Liz

cues.text: Right - as you say, all very logical.
cues.speaker: Sam
